stories.body:
If you’ve spent any time on social media recently, you’ve probably found yourself wondering whether you should be taking a magnesium supplement. There’s no shortage of influencers listing all the benefits that different types of magnesium supplements have – from boosting brain function to helping ease anxiety and improving sleep.

Indeed, magnesium is an essential mineral involved in hundreds of processes in the body. It helps muscles and nerves work properly, supports energy production and contributes to the maintenance of strong bones and teeth.

Magnesium is also important for maintaining a healthy heart rhythm, regulating blood pressure and blood sugar levels. Many people don’t get enough from their diet , so supplements can be useful in some situations.

But when you look closely at the research, there’s little evidence to suggest that any one type of magnesium supplement has unique benefits over another.

Magnesium glycinate

One of the most talked about types of magnesium is magnesium glycinate, often promoted as the best option for sleep. This form combines magnesium with glycine , an amino acid that may improve sleep on its own.

While some research does show that magnesium may improve sleep , these trials do not show that glycinate is any better than other forms. Glycinate’s main advantage is that it’s gentle on the stomach and well absorbed , which may make it easier for some people to tolerate.

Magnesium L-threonate

Another form that attracts a lot of attention is magnesium L-threonate. It’s suggested it can improve memory and focus.

These claims appear to come from early animal studies which suggested that L-threonate may increase magnesium levels in the brain more effectively than other forms. In these studies, which were conducted in rats, supplementation enhanced several types of memory and increased the number and function of connections between brain cells in the hippocampus – a key region involved in learning and memory.

Human evidence remains relatively limited. One study did demonstrate that in people who took 2g of L-threonate daily for six weeks, the supplement was associated with improvements in several areas of thinking and memory – including working memory, memory of past events, reaction speed and overall mental performance.

But as the supplement was only compared against a placebo, the results cannot tell us whether L-threonate is more effective than other magnesium supplements when it comes to brain function.

Magnesium malate

Magnesium malate combines magnesium with malic acid, a compound involved in energy production within cells . Magnesium malate is often promoted for its purported ability to support energy levels and muscle function.

Magnesium in general is important for normal muscle and nerve function . Correcting a deficiency can improve symptoms such as fatigue and muscle cramps. But there’s little evidence that magnesium malate offers advantages over other magnesium formulations – except that it’s absorbed well .

Some small studies in people with fibromyalgia (a condition which causes widespread pain, extreme tiredness and problems with sleep) have reported that malate is associated with improvements in pain and fatigue. But there’s currently no strong evidence that malate is superior to other well-absorbed forms of magnesium when it comes to improving muscle function or energy levels in the general population.

Magnesium citrate and oxide

Forms such as magnesium citrate and magnesium oxide are often used for constipation because magnesium draws water into the bowel.

Both forms may also reduce the severity and frequency of migraines and are cost-effective options. However, the oxide form is absorbed less efficiently, so people may need higher doses to achieve the same effect as citrate, which may cause an upset stomach.

Final verdict

Overall, across a range of clinical trials, magnesium has shown some benefits for sleep quality, anxiety symptoms , migraines and blood pressure . But there’s no strong evidence that one form is better than another.

Many online claims that one types is more beneficial than another usually come from small pilot studies, animal research or supplement marketing – rather than large, well-designed human trials. Direct comparisons between different magnesium salts are lacking, so more research is needed to find out whether some types of magnesium do really work better than others.

While magnesium is beneficial for our health, it’s worth asking whether supplements are even necessary. For most people, a varied and balanced diet is the best way to get magnesium. Foods with naturally high levels of magnesium include leafy greens (such as spinach and kale), nuts and seeds, wholegrains and beans. These foods provide fibre, antioxidants and other nutrients that supplements cannot offer. They also reduce the risk of taking too much magnesium, which can cause diarrhoea or stomach upset .

Those most likely to benefit from a magnesium supplement include people diagnosed with a deficiency, people with certain medical conditions (such as Crohn’s disease, which affects the body’s ability to absorb nutrients from food) and people who struggle to get enough magnesium from their diet.

For those who may benefit from a magnesium supplement, it’s worth noting that some forms of magnesium – particularly magnesium citrate and glycinate – appear to be more readily absorbed by the body than others. Magnesium citrate is also recommended for treating a deficiency .

So even if two supplements contain the same amount of magnesium, the body may absorb more from one than the other. Factors including the dose and the presence of other nutrients (such as potassium and vitamin B6) can also affect absorption .

For most people, improving diet is a more sustainable approach to boosting magnesium levels.

stories.body:
In Happy Days, one of Irish playwright Samuel Beckett’s best-known plays, the body of the protagonist Winnie is embedded in a mound of sand or dirt. During the first act, she is buried to above her waist and in the second, she is buried up to her neck.

In the stage directions, Beckett specifies the staging should feature an “expanse of scorched grass rising centre to low mound”, as well as “blazing light”. This is suggestive of a post-human landscape which has been affected by ecological disaster.

Beckett’s works have been labelled absurd, existentialist, modern and postmodern by critics. Yet the setting presented in Happy Days (first performed in 1961) feels uniquely contemporary in our age of ongoing climate crisis .

Born in Dublin in 1906, some of Beckett’s earliest interactions with nature took place on local walks. Often joining his father William on lengthy excursions around the Dublin hills to avoid the religious obligation of Sunday church, these early ambles helped to imprint the landscape on his artistic consciousness. Images from these walks subsequently found their way into a number of his literary works.

Yet it was much later, after Beckett had abandoned a promising academic career to move to Paris and become a writer, that he encountered serious ecological and human destruction.

With the outbreak of the second world war, he joined the French resistance before becoming a member of the ambulance corps, based in the Normandy town of Saint-Lô. As biographer James Knowlson recalls in Damned To Fame: The Life of Samuel Beckett (1996), it was here that:

Beckett witnessed real devastation and misery … Possessions blown to pieces; a ward full of patients ill with tuberculosis … People in desperate need of food and clothing, yet clinging desperately onto life; a hospital created out of nothing on fields that became churned into a sea of mud.

My PhD research at the University of Liverpool explores Beckett’s work. The university hosts a biennial festival dedicated to his life and works. The current iteration, Beckett: Lieben 2026 , features stagings, musical interpretations, photography, visual art and talks related to Beckett’s experiences in Germany.

Staging Happy Days

First performed 16 years after the end of the war, Happy Days features little sign of human civilisation in the near-empty, barren landscape that the two protagonists Winnie and Willie inhabit.

Winnie shows a desperation to cling on to life despite the constrictions of the mound, shown through her incessant activity. She frequently rummages through her bag, for example, because it is one of her only remaining means of autonomy.

Within the earth that constricts her body, Winnie’s only remaining signs of life are her physical movements and, in the second act, her words. In a contemporary sense, action and communication are vital tools for engaging effectively with our ecological crisis, before the situation worsens and the fiction of Winnie’s environmental collapse becomes a reality.

This article is part of Rethinking the Classics . The stories in this series offer insightful new ways to think about and interpret classic books and artworks. This is the canon – with a twist.

During rehearsals of Happy Days at the Royal Court Theatre in 1979, Beckett insisted to the scholar Martha Fehsenfeld that Winnie is “like a bird with oil on its feathers”.

Such an image feels damning in today’s world, where oil spills occur frequently and animals often bear the marks of human ecological irresponsibility. The comment underlines that Winnie’s paralysis is symbolic of how environmental damage affects animals as well as humans.

Rather than placing her in a mound, Katie Mitchell’s 2015 production of the play in Hamburg, Germany situated Winnie in a kitchen, with rising water threatening to engulf her body.

Beckett’s ambiguous setting, in which the rising mound gradually envelops Winnie’s body, echoes other ecological issues – be it the rising water levels which threaten to erode our coastlines, or the rising flames of forest fires which threaten to enclose our trees and kill our biodiversity.

Seeing or reading Happy Days in the light of frequent ecological disasters, audiences are reminded that Winnie’s body is inextricable from the earth in which it is buried – just as human bodies are inseparable from the Earth we inhabit.

Thus, Happy Days serves as a necessary reminder to look after our planet while we still can – if we are to avoid our bodies becoming engulfed by disaster, like Winnie’s.

Beyond the canon

As part of the Rethinking the Classics series, we’re asking our experts to recommend a book or artwork that tackles similar themes to the canonical work in question, but isn’t (yet) considered a classic itself. Here is Fraser Cattini’s suggestion:

For fans of Happy Days, I would recommend the art of Ana Mendieta (1948-1985). As a Cuban multimedia artist, Mendieta created performances, videos, sculptures and photographs with a particular focus on the relationship between body and landscape. Her works incorporate a range of natural materials such as blood, dirt, moss and feathers.

Her 1974 work Burial Pyramid draws remarkable similarities with Beckett’s aesthetics. In this 3½-minute video, Mendieta is buried beneath a pile of rocks – recalling the pre-Columbian, Indigenous Cuban tradition of honouring and protecting the dead by burying them beneath stones. As the video progresses, the rocks begin to fall away, revealing Mendieta’s naked body enshrouded in dirt.

Mendieta’s performance draws attention to the colonial past of her native Cuba, as well as the mistreatment of women by colonial powers. The relationship between her body and the land in which she is buried becomes an important signifier of heritage, and a vital marker of identity.

stories.body:
ProPublica revealed that the FBI was circling Sen. Collins over a defense contractor’s donations — until President Trump gutted the unit in charge. Collins has since mustered a defense with a series of incorrect and misleading claims.

As the scandal over Susan Collins’ relationship with Hawaii defense contractor Navatek became the central issue in her hotly contested senate campaign, she and her top aides mustered a defense with a series of incorrect and misleading claims.

Read More

On Tuesday, ProPublica published an investigation into the senior senator from Maine’s relationship with Martin Kao, the former Navatek CEO and a major donor who told law enforcement he exchanged campaign cash for government contracts. His confession came after his guilty plea for campaign finance and loan fraud.

The ProPublica story revealed that the FBI had been circling the senator, her top aides and a pro-Collins super PAC in recent years, asking questions about their relationship with Navatek. Since returning to office, President Donald Trump fired or pushed out most of the federal agents and lawyers investigating high-profile federal corruption matters, including those working on the Kao case. The dismissals ended the corruption review, which was in its early stages.

After the story published, Collins and her campaign denied any wrongdoing in numerous media appearances. Some of the statements made by Collins and her representatives are not accurate.

Collins : “In 2021, the Biden Justice Department found there was no wrongdoing by anyone on my campaign staff, my office or me.”

Collins : “The Biden-led Justice Department and FBI totally cleared my office, my campaign and me five years ago of these seven-year-old allegations.”

An FBI spokesperson told ProPublica the agency had investigated claims against Collins years ago “and ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign.”

But the investigation at the center of ProPublica’s story was based on claims Kao made between 2022 through 2024 — not seven years ago, as Collins states. That investigation did not conclude under President Joe Biden but under Trump, in 2025, after his administration purged the agents and Department of Justice attorneys assigned to the case.

Collins is referring to the FBI’s initial investigation of Kao, which started in 2021. No one in Collins’ orbit was charged as a result of that earlier investigation.

FBI records reviewed by ProPublica show the agency remained interested in the conduct of Collins and her staff right up until the most recent phase of their investigation was shut down under Trump.

The documents show that Kao was still answering agents’ questions as late as September 2024, when he sat for a two-day interview with FBI agents at the U.S. attorney’s office in Honolulu. During that interview, Kao provided them with a 50-page document offering many new allegations about his interactions with elected officials, including Collins.

And in early 2025, FBI agents were still examining Kao’s relationship with Collins, her staffers and employees of the super PAC, ProPublica found.

Annie Clark, deputy chief of staff to Collins : “The FBI and the Court obviously did not believe Kao.”

The judge in Kao’s sentencing ultimately offered him no benefit for his cooperation with federal authorities, sentencing him to 87 months in federal prison. While Kao had credibility issues — as a convicted felon — FBI documents seen by ProPublica show that agents were able to corroborate some of his claims.

“Pursuant to a Grand Jury Subpoena issued to Navatek, related to the previous investigation, hundreds of thousands of documents were provided to the FBI,” agents wrote in a December 2024 document.

“Several emails and other documents corroborate Kao’s statements made to the FBI.”

In addition, people familiar with the investigation told ProPublica that FBI agents found Kao to be credible.

Clark : “ProPublica took the word of someone who pled guilty to five counts of money laundering, three counts of wire fraud, one count of bank fraud, and making false submissions to the FEC.”

ProPublica did not simply take Kao at his word but reviewed a trove of evidence gathered by the FBI. It also examined thousands of pages of legal records and interviewed dozens of people familiar with Navatek, its Washington operations and the FBI inquiry to independently corroborate much of Kao’s account.

For instance, Kao said that Scott Reed, the head of the Collins super PAC, promised to make the senator aware that Kao was the person behind a large, anonymous donation to the super PAC made through a shell company.

We published emails between Reed and Kao showing that Kao told Reed the name of the shell company he was using to anonymize his $150,000 donation. And we included an email from someone working for Reed to a Navatek representative asking for Kao’s number so Collins could thank him for the donation. These are consistent with Kao’s version of events.

Steve Abbott, Collins’ campaign manager, said at a Wednesday press conference, “We have no record of her calling him.” But he added that such a phone call would not be unusual: “We routinely thank people for contributions. … We try to thank everybody.”

Reed did not answer detailed questions about the $150,000 donation but said he didn’t speak to Collins about Kao. He added, “I understand Martin Kao is now sitting in federal prison.”

Do You Have Information About Political Dealmaking in Washington?

We’re still reporting on pay-for-play arrangements between powerful companies and elected officials.

stories.title: The Federal Agency That’s Supposed to Protect Consumers Just Made Another Business-Friendly Move
stories.summary: The post The Federal Agency That’s Supposed to Protect Consumers Just Made Another Business-Friendly Move appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: The CFPB logo on glass. Out of focus behind the logo, “CFPB” appears on a wall near a metal detector and a flag. Rows of circular lights line the ceiling.
stories.body:
Debt collection. Credit reporting. Payday loans. Consumer complaints to a federal database used to help reveal issues and bring accountability. Then the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau stopped publishing the narratives.

Every year, millions of complaints flow to the federal Consumer Financial Protection Bureau from people across the country. The complaints, which range in focus from debt collection to credit reporting to payday loans and more, long served as a window into Americans’ gripes and struggles with various companies.

For over a decade, consumers could opt in to have what they wrote published as public information in a CFPB database. But last month, the Trump administration announced that it would stop publishing those complaint narratives , a decision that aligns the agency with corporations that have critiqued the system for years.

“Publishing such narratives in the Database provides a less-than-representative sample of one-sided experiences,” the CFPB said in a press release.

In the big picture, the move is part of a trend of the administration taking a friendlier approach with businesses — even at the federal agency tasked with guarding consumers from unfair and deceptive practices.

The complaint system helps consumers get responses from companies about their problems, and sometimes even fixes. It has also given the public — as well as federal investigators and regulators— access to information that serves as a warning or to help spot problems.

As a ProPublica data reporter, I’ve used the complaints time and time again as a tool for accountability-driven reporting. I appreciated reading about people’s raw frustration, written in their own words, which can often point to larger trends. It was a rare federal dataset that captured human emotions. Some were grievances like being unable to get help after spending far too much time calling or emailing customer service. Sometimes complaints had more urgency: desperation to fix crushing high-interest debt, a frozen bank account or a credit score tanked from a reporting error.

With the recent loss of a crucial piece of the public database, I wanted to share with you some of ProPublica’s reporting using those complaints. And, while these stories about financial harm have often led to some accountability, revisiting the complaints also offers a taste of what we’ll be missing.

1. A Wisconsin Tribe Built a Lending Empire Charging 600% Annual Rates to Borrowers

I’ve used the complaints to report on high-interest tribal loans that skirt state interest rate caps to charge 600% interest or more. CFPB complaints helped point me and my colleague Megan O’Matz to an opaque but massive lending operation based in Wisconsin , which we estimated to be involved in thousands of bankruptcies nationwide each year.

“THIS IS THE TEXTBOOK DEFINITION ON LOANSHARKING.” Consumer complaint about a tribal loan company, June 2023

The borrower also argued that “no one should be expected to pay over $11,000 for a $1,200 loan,” calling the 790% rate “beyond predatory.”

In emails to ProPublica, the tribe’s president, John Johnson Sr., defended the tribe’s lending business as legal and said the loans help people “without access to traditional financial services.” He added that many borrowers have had positive experiences.

A few months after ProPublica reported on the operation, the tribe settled a civil suit filed by Minnesota’s attorney general. The tribe denied the allegations but agreed to stop lending to Minnesotans and forgive outstanding loans to the state’s residents.

2. Credit Bureaus Are Leaving More Mistakes on Frustrated Consumers’ Reports Under Trump’s CFPB

In March, I reported that two of the big three credit bureaus, Experian and TransUnion, provided relief to a substantially smaller portion of consumers last year. The credit bureaus are by far the most common subject of consumers’ woes in the database, with over 4 million complaints filed about them in 2025.

A Texan filed a complaint to each of the three credit bureaus, Experian, Equifax and TransUnion, writing that a fraudulent account remained on their credit report despite their disputes:

“I have an important deal that I need to complete that is important for the safety and survival of my family, and this issue has damaged my credit score.” Consumer complaint, August 2025

In response to the story, four Democratic senators wrote letters to the credit bureaus demanding answers on how they handle disputes and complaints. The CFPB’s acting director at the time, Russell Vought, also tacitly acknowledged the reporting during his congressional testimony in July, saying that “with credit reporting agencies we saw things in the news that were concerning to us. We reached out to them.”

The credit bureaus did not comment on specific complaints, but told ProPublica that many complaints are illegitimate, including a large volume filed by credit repair organizations that charge customers to challenge negative information on their reports. (CFPB records show that Equifax provided relief in response to the Texan’s complaint, while TransUnion and Experian did not.)

3. The Trump Administration’s Plan for Protecting Consumers? Politely Ask Companies to Behave.

Last month, my colleague Andy Kroll reported on the Trump CFPB’s light-touch approach to oversight, focusing on its ask-nicely strategy of holding the fintech startup Bilt accountable after it threw users’ accounts into chaos twice in quick succession. The story included complaints about how Bilt’s artificial intelligence support system gave information that was:

“ completely wrong ” and “ demonstrably … false. ” Consumer complaints about Bilt, March and April 2026

(In a statement at the time, Bilt said its new card had “attracted unexpectedly high demand, and some of our members experienced gaps in service that are simply unacceptable to us.” The company told ProPublica it resolved all problems related to the new cards “months ago.” The CFPB did not respond to any questions or requests for comment.)

Kroll’s recent story also examined how the agency has changed under the Trump administration. Under Vought’s leadership, the CFPB attempted to fire roughly 90% of its staff in April 2025 before a federal court ruling stymied the move. When the efforts to dismantle the agency failed, Vought and his allies instead refashioned it into an industry-friendly regulator.

The loss of the public complaint narratives is another example of that. And it is a win for groups such as the Consumer Data Industry Association, which represents the credit bureaus and has argued that publishing complaint narratives would “harm the brands of legitimate, law-abiding companies” by presenting unverified, self-selected negative anecdotes. More recently, the group argued in a January public comment letter that the complaint portal has become “a sort of ‘Yelp for Financial Services,’” and that the CFPB doesn’t have the authority to publish complaint data in the first place.

Although the CFPB has been subject to partisan fights, the complaint system has been used by Americans across the country. GOP lawmakers even referred thousands of constituents to the CFPB’s complaint system to get help. Still, those same lawmakers voted last year to slash the agency’s budget by nearly half.

While the complaint system is required by law, the agency isn’t mandated to make it public. In theory, a future administration could go back to publishing the complaint narratives, but the agency has removed the option for consumers to consent to making public what they wrote. That means that any complaints filed in the near term cannot be retroactively published. The complaint narratives will still be subject to Freedom of Information Act requests, but getting them could be time-consuming and challenging .

As the CFPB turns away from its watchdog role, it’s making it harder for all of us to watch as well.

stories.title: Why China Will Rule AI
stories.summary: The post Why China Will Rule AI appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Open societies are at a disadvantage.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

In his 2013 book, “The End of Power,” Moisés Naim famously wrote that “power no longer buys as much as it did in the past. In the twenty-first century, power is easier to get, harder to use—and easier to lose.”

That may be true for deconstructed authority in the West, but it is not true in China where the weighty center of authority remains in the un-deconstructed Communist Party. There, power is hard for others to get, easily used and nearly impossible ever to lose.

This systemic incapacity of open societies puts them at a disadvantage when it comes to ruling frontier AI models.

Endless appeals about the dangers of unleashed AI from rosters of the most eminent scientists, Papal encyclicals and monarchical meditations gain no effective traction. The public is warily confused and feels helpless to affect the set course of events. By and large, legislators appear hopelessly clueless and slow on the draw as AI development exponentially accelerates.

The dire warnings and calls for regulation by the top CEOs of Big Tech are suspect as a ruse to create a cartel of the most powerful to keep competitors at bay. The “leader of the free world” simply dismisses any and all worries as nothing more than a “hoax” that will prevent America from becoming great again.

Everyone throws in their two cents or two trillion and then throws up their hands in virtual resignation. At the end of the day, there is no core institution or vested authority that can impose control over AIs demonstrably capable of escaping their programmed confines. Unable to reach consensus out of the cacophony of voices and welter of conflicting interests, the best we can hope for — if that — is a pause in the pace toward the precipice by the AI companies themselves.

The Chinese government, by contrast, is taking the reins firmly in hand with few qualms. In China, “human alignment” of AIs equals ideological alignment with the Party, which will resolutely thwart any threat to its enduring dominance by superintelligent machines.

The AI Threats China Sees

Even as official propaganda accuses Western warnings about loss of control of AIs as “fear-mongering,” China’s Minister of State Security, Chen Yixin, last week made crystal clear where the lines would be drawn. In an article published in Chinese media, he listed the key threats to “political” and “ideological security,” cybersecurity, espionage and “military struggle.”

It is worth reading the list to get a sense of how those in charge in China see the AI challenge:

“First, AI has a systemic impact on the political and security environment. As of June 2026, the number of users of artificial intelligence products in China exceeded 500 million, with daily word meta-calls exceeding 140 trillion, and the application of artificial intelligence has been rapidly and comprehensively deployed. Various hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives abuse generative artificial intelligence technologies such as deepfake audio and video, AI-generated text and images, and intelligent online trolls to fabricate political rumors, spread harmful information, and incite confrontational sentiments at low cost and in large quantities, waging a propaganda war and a cognitive war against us, directly threatening our political security, institutional security, and ideological security. Read Noema in print.

Second, the cybersecurity landscape is undergoing a disruptive upgrade. Marked by recent developments in large-scale models like “Claude Mythos” and “GPT-5.5-Cyber” by US tech companies, artificial intelligence technology is significantly improving the efficiency and weaponization of network vulnerability discovery and malware development. Cybersecurity is entering a new phase characterized by vulnerability industrialization, fully automated attack and defense, and AI versus AI. Some countries and organizations possess the capability to rapidly and in large quantities discover vulnerabilities, automatically connect attack paths, and complete complex hacking tasks, drastically lowering the technical barriers and costs of launching cyberattacks and posing serious risks to China’s critical information infrastructure.

“In China, ‘human alignment’ of AIs equals ideological alignment with the Party, which will resolutely thwart any threat to its enduring dominance by superintelligent machines.”

Third, the risk of large-scale espionage and leaks is amplified. Foreign intelligence agencies are extensively using technologies such as intelligent web crawlers, intelligent data mining, and intelligent profiling to collect and acquire sensitive information such as key national data, trade secrets, and citizens’ personal privacy. Some domestic users lack sufficient security awareness, using foreign AI products to process sensitive information and export data overseas, resulting in large-scale data leaks from within the country. Even open-source AI tools like “Lobster,” [the Chinese nickname for OpenClaw] which became wildly popular in the first half of 2026, suffer from structural problems such as remote control of device management permissions and leakage of sensitive user information.

Fourth, monopolistic practices exacerbate the imbalance in technological development. Some countries, leveraging their accumulated advantages in basic artificial intelligence theories, model architectures, and core computing power, use the pretext of “maintaining national security” to strictly restrict the introduction of cutting-edge technologies and equipment and the enhancement of technological innovation capabilities by means of establishing entity lists, implementing technology controls, monopolizing industry standards, and creating closed-source ecosystems. This fragments the global artificial intelligence industry chain and supply chain, exacerbating the imbalance in the development of the global intelligent industry.

Fifth, it has a structural impact on the social governance system. The application of artificial intelligence brings a large number of uncertainties to social governance and public order. The “black box” of algorithms and the “poisoning” of data may amplify existing social biases. The abuse of personal information during data use may trigger a crisis of user trust. The automatic decision-making of the system creates problems in attribution of responsibility. In particular, the rapid development of artificial intelligence has broken through the traditional technology governance framework, causing existing legal norms, ethical principles and governance mechanisms to frequently lag behind in practice, making it difficult to form an effective institutional constraint and supervision system.

Sixth, it fundamentally transforms the form of military struggle. Artificial intelligence technology is propelling warfare into an intelligent era. Whoever can achieve more refined perception, more accurate judgment, and more precise strikes through algorithms will gain the initiative on the battlefield. For example, in the US-Israel-Iran conflict, the militarized application of artificial intelligence has spurred the intelligent fusion of intelligence, intelligent decision-making assistance, intelligent target identification, intelligent support for actual combat, and intelligent shaping of cognition. Artificial intelligence is transforming from a ‘supporting role’ on the battlefield into a ‘key role.’”

Dissident AI Agents & Embedded Evaluators

The message is clear enough. No dissident AI agents with “ulterior motives” will be allowed to collude, break out and challenge the material security of the state or the ideological security of the governing narrative through inciting “confrontational sentiments.” Any AI company whose models even approach that threshold knows what happened to Alibaba CEO Jack Ma. He thought it wise to decamp to Tokyo when the Party made clear to him who was in ultimate control once the e-commerce giant got too powerful.

One safeguard remedy proposed by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is to place independent “embedded evaluators” in AI companies as a check against losing control of frontier models. China already has that in spades: AI companies of any consequence must have an embedded Party cell that keeps watch internally to ensure conformity with Party directives and remind them who, in the end, is the boss.

As has often been reported, China has focused more on developing and diffusing practical applications of AI and less so on building ever-more powerful frontier models. Where they are pursuing that objective as a matter of strategic imperative, those models will not be the proprietary province of private interests but tightly corralled and protected by the Party-state security apparatus.

The asymmetry with open societies is stark. China has the central political authority, institutions, managed social consensus and ready policy instruments to rule AIs that the West is lacking. History will tell which is the better match for superintelligence.

stories.title: Russia Expands Its War
stories.summary: And European leaders are freaking out. The post Russia Expands Its War appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Strasbourg, France (Shutterstock)

European leaders are now fretting about Vladimir Putin in much the same way that everyone worries these days about artificial intelligence.

Until recently, AI agents remained within the virtual spaces where they’d been developed. Rather than free range, they were confined to their “sandboxes.” But there have been a number of cases of these AI agents lying, cheating, and hacking their way out of their designated spaces. Now, even AI experts are talking about the not-insignificant odds that the technology they designed will run amok and kill all of humanity.

Putin, too, was at the beginning of his reign confined to his Russian sandbox. Then he intervened in Georgia. He lied and cheated his way into Crimea and the Donbas. In 2022, he expanded Russian operations significantly when he tried to take over all of Ukraine.

Still, from the European point of view, Russia was flexing its muscles within the post-Soviet space. Now, Russian agents are increasingly operating outside this sandbox as well to launch attacks elsewhere in Europe. They have hired single-use operatives to commit arson, which would likely include such recent attacks as the one on WB Electronics , a Polish manufacturer of drones for Ukraine. An attack drone, which failed to detonate, was found last month at the Leipzig airport near a Ukrainian transport plane. There have been an estimated 150 Russian-linked cases of sabotage throughout Europe between 2022 and 2026, and the pace of the attacks is accelerating.

Russia is already involved in what NATO calls “out-of-area operations.” So far, however, these operations remain within a grey zone of sort-of plausible deniability. But European leaders are concerned that Putin, too, has the capacity to run amok and trigger a world war, if not a nuclear apocalypse.

The most recent cause for concern was the military exercise that Belarus conducted last week near its borders with Poland and Lithuania. This is the infamous Suwalki Gap, the narrow wedge of territory that separates Belarus from the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad and that connects the Baltic countries to the rest of NATO. During the Cold War, NATO ran various war games in anticipation of a Soviet attack on Poland through this 65-mile gap. Now, NATO leaders worry that Russia, perhaps alongside Belarus, will manufacture some excuse to “defend” Kaliningrad by occupying part of Lithuania or Poland.

After that, as former presidential envoy Brett McGurk imagines the scenario, “Russia would also claim through non-official channels that a NATO response risked nuclear war. The purpose is less about the Gap and severing NATO’s Baltic flank, than undermining NATO and its mutual defense commitments altogether.”

European leaders are freaking out. Polish leader Donald Tusk has reported on intelligence assessments that Russia is planning an attack on NATO in the next months. Emmanuel Macron recently brought together all French party leaders and prospective presidential candidates to discuss this threat. Finland has tested its civil defense shelters for the first time in 30 years (though the Finnish prime minister has also cautioned his European colleagues not to overreact to Russian actions).

Even the otherwise Russia-friendly Trump administration is getting a little worried.

Though Trump has threatened to pull U.S. troops out of European countries for their failure to support his various military ventures—and removed 5,000 troops from Germany in the spring—he is moving forward with establishing a new U.S. military base in Poland, which the Poles tout as vital for countering Russia. One reason for the dispatch of CIA chief John Ratcliffe to Moscow last month was reportedly to warn the Kremlin not to attack NATO members. And the Justice Department has charged five Russian intelligence operatives with belonging to a network that “paid and attempted to pay individuals within the United States and elsewhere to conduct pre-operational surveillance and carry out targeted killings, and commissioned associates to commit and attempt to commit acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that are aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine.”

Putin’s Plans

At a certain level, none of this makes sense.

To date, Russia has scrupulously avoided any engagement with NATO forces for fear that the latter, if they intervened directly in the conflict, would tip the war in favor of Ukraine. Now more than ever, Russia can’t afford such a confrontation. The war inside Ukraine is not going well for Russian forces. So far in 2026, Ukraine has clawed back 375 square miles , which includes 60 settlements. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure is having a serious impact on the Russian economy, with refining capacity cut nearly in half , billions of dollars in lost export revenues, and gas prices soaring at home. The war is now having a direct impact on Russian wallets, and that could mean political problems (at some point) for Putin.

The Russian president doesn’t harbor ambitions to take over Europe. Nor does he want to reconstitute the old Soviet Union. Even reestablishing control over the relatively small Baltic states—Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia—would pose enormous challenges either in the form of a NATO response or guerrilla resistance to Russian military rule.

Instead, what Putin wants is to control the fates of the regions surrounding Russia. In the Kremlin’s best-case scenario, Russian incorporates the predominantly Russian-speaking areas of the “near abroad,” like parts of eastern Ukraine and eastern Latvia. Putin has also drawn together semi-autonomous regions like Transnistria in Moldova and Abkhazia in Georgia into a League of Unrecognized Territories. He has locked down the allegiances of fully independent governments—Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, and the current government in Georgia—that look to Russia for trade and protection. The Kremlin invested a lot of money and time into backing a pro-Russian party in Moldova that, if it had won in the election this year, could have dragged the country in that same direction.

But Putin would also be content with dividing, politically paralyzing, and economically devastating the recalcitrant states on its borders to make sure that they aren’t cohesive enough to join NATO or, more importantly, the European Union. Putin is currently pursuing that fall-back option in Ukraine.

Ukraine hasn’t yet knuckled under. So, Putin is simultaneously pursuing another option. If Ukraine can’t be divided and conquered then perhaps pressure can be brought to bear on the other side of the equation. And so, Putin is testing the cohesion of both NATO and the EU. The grey-zone attacks against NATO targets is one way of testing how resolute the alliance really is, especially now, when the Trump administration has expressed doubts about the Article 5 collective defense mechanism.

The recent victories of the Alternative for Deutschland in the Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern regional elections—and the party’s commanding lead in national polling—point to another way for Putin to compromise the EU now that his finger puppet Viktor Orban is no longer in charge in Hungary. The AfD has not been shy in touting its pro-Russian policies. It is already preparing for talks with the Russian government in early 2027 to lay the groundwork for restarting German imports of natural gas.

Putin, meanwhile, has consolidated his power on the home front. In elections this month, Putin’s United Russia party won a record number of seats in the Duma. Putin has sidelined—silenced, arrested, exiled, killed—all serious political opposition. Like Stalin, he has gone after critics on the left and the right. He has also rejected all ceasefire proposals and appears to be on the verge of calling up another several hundred thousand new recruits for the war in Ukraine.

Despite Ukrainian successes on the battlefield and its drone war against Russian infrastructure, Putin feels fully in control. At least until 2027, he is likely to continue to wage war in Ukraine to secure all of the Donbas, and he will also continue to pursue grey-zone operations in Europe.

International condemnation of Russia hasn’t been even a speed bump for Putin. Military assistance to Ukraine has leveled the battlefield, to an extent, but it also hasn’t stopped the Russian leader. Sanctions have wreaked havoc on the Russian economy, but they haven’t brought down the country’s military industrial complex.

Trump, meanwhile, has tried maximum appeasement, from the red-carpet treatment in Alaska extended to Putin to the incorporation of Russian talking points in the peace plan presented by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Ukraine has refused to go along with this strategy.

That leaves three options.

Western Options

The West could maintain its current policy of refusing to provide Ukraine with a significant military advantage. The war will continue to take its terrible toll without either side able to declare definitive victory. Maybe that will produce an armistice, along the Korean War model. Maybe it will just produce a forever war along with an uptick in mysterious attacks on European targets.

Or the Trump administration could put maximum pressure on Ukraine to buckle diplomatically and accept Russian terms in an unequal peace deal. This would not be a just solution and, given Ukrainian obstinance to date, it probably wouldn’t work either.

The last option is not very palatable. In response to grey-zone attacks, NATO could present Putin with an ultimatum backed by a credible threat of force (for instance, a no-fly zone over Ukraine). I’m no fan of NATO, and I worry about escalation to the nuclear level. But given that Putin seems to understand only the language of power, some show of force by the West could make the Russian leader think twice about further expanding his war. It might also push Russia to the negotiating table.

Putin thinks that he has time on his side. He has near-absolute control over his country and can sacrifice pretty much everything to the war effort. If he waits long enough—and continues to use his asymmetric advantage to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure—the West might succumb to its many divisions and lose both the will and capacity to support Ukraine. Or Putin’s out-of-sandbox operations, like the recent misdemeanors of AI agents, has the potential to unite the world against the rising threat.

The super-intelligence of AI, the middling intelligence of Putin, and the sub-intelligence of Trump: the world now faces an unholy trinity of supervillains.

stories.title: Let The People Set The Pace Of Frontier AI
stories.summary: The post Let The People Set The Pace Of Frontier AI appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Slogans won’t slow the rapid development of dangerously powerful AI. But a citizens’ assembly representative of humanity’s diversity and independent of frontier labs and national governments could.

Hélène Landemore is the Damon Wells ‘58 professor of political science at Yale University and distinguished researcher at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI.

Audrey Tang is Taiwan’s cyber ambassador and founding minister of digital affairs, a Carnegie distinguished fellow at Columbia University School of International and Public Affairs, a senior fellow at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI, a senior research fellow at the Collective Intelligence Project and a 2025 Right Livelihood Laureate.

Those building the most powerful AI systems in the world are increasingly telling us that the race to build them may be moving too fast. But there is a problem: They cannot simply agree to slow down.

On Sept. 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for an easing of the pace at which AI models improve and committed his company to giving independent, third-party evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to its systems. Amodei further gestured toward “democratic coordination” on shared safety limits and “global coordination” on the international stage. Within hours, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed that “we need to pace the frontier” and made the same evaluator pledge. Elon Musk’s response was three words: “Dario is right.”

This apparent convergence among the leaders of the frontier AI labs is striking. It comes after months of mounting concern inside and outside the industry: AI models have begun to find ways around safeguards and test environments; researchers have left frontier labs amid disagreements over catastrophic and extinction-level risks; and more than 1,300 employees at leading AI companies have called on Washington to back an international slowdown.

But even if the CEOs agree, the race does not stop.

The reason is structural. The two governments with the greatest capacity to shape the frontier AI race — in Washington and Beijing — have powerful incentives not to be the first to slow down. Each has reason to fear that restraint on their part will simply hand a strategic advantage to the other.

What we are facing, in other words, is a double collective-action problem, one nested under the other. The two are linked: “If we slow down, China wins” is the main argument American labs and government officials use against binding regulation. The outer race is the inner one’s best excuse; end the global race, and the domestic one loses cover. The good news is that, contrary to frequent depictions, neither is a simple prisoner’s dilemma, in which each player’s best strategy is to defect no matter what others do, and also that the only solution is necessarily some sort of global regulatory leviathan.

Instead, both collective-action problems look more like what game theorists call a “stag hunt,” after a parable of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s. A party of hunters sets out after a stag. It will take all of them to bring it down, and it will feed them all for days. Along the way, each hunter sees a hare and considers catching it. The hare is a thin meal but a sure one, though if even a single hunter breaks off to chase one, the stag escapes and the rest go home hungry. Nobody in the party prefers the hare. A hunter settles for it only after losing faith that the others will hold the line in the quest for the stag.

The stag, here, is a frontier paced long enough to make safe; the hare is the lead a single lab or a single country can take by racing on alone. A lab or a country that trusted its rivals would do better by pacing alongside them, since a shared slowdown is worth more than a temporary lead that might ruin everyone, the leader included.

“The two governments with the greatest capacity to shape the frontier AI race have powerful incentives not to be the first to slow down.”

The way out of a stag hunt is not coercion but an assurance mechanism. If each player can believe that the others will keep their post and, even better, watch them keeping to their posts, the fear that pulls the party apart loses its grip. The frontier does not have to be placed under a single world power to be slowed down and controlled. But it needs assurance, and assurance requires two things: verification and a witness that is credible to all parties.

The first is already taking shape. The independent evaluators Anthropic and OpenAI pledged to permit would see inside frontier systems with employee-like access and could report whether a lab is keeping its pace. But evaluators engaged by the labs, judging against risk thresholds the labs themselves define, cannot reassure a rival, let alone a rival government. Evidence changes what the hunters believe about one another only when it flows to someone none of them controls, and who has set the standard it is measured against.

What is needed to nudge all players toward the cooperative equilibrium, therefore, is a body with enough moral authority to be an obvious coordination point and with the political legitimacy to set the terms of cooperation, coordinate the verification process and raise the reputational costs for any form of defection. What existing body has such moral authority and political legitimacy in the world today?

The obvious candidate is the United Nations, which is the closest thing we have to a standing witness for the world’s affairs. But the U.N. is not a neutral bystander here: It is structurally entangled with the very powers whose rivalry drives the race. The Security Council grants Washington and Beijing each a veto over the institution meant to referee them. More deeply, the U.N. is built out of nation-states and speaks in their voice and language. It is an assembly of sovereigns, not a body that can stand above sovereignty and weigh it against humanity’s interests.

If not the U.N., then who? One contender has a stronger claim than any institution, on this issue and many others: humanity itself, whose interests, and indeed survival, are crucially at stake in whether the race continues unabated or is tamed. Humanity alone stands above AI CEOs, the governments in Washington and Beijing, other competing nations, international boards of experts and even the U.N. in its credibility to say “Stop!” or “Slow down” or “We want AI to do this but not that.” That is because humanity’s stake is universal and undiluted by any single national or corporate interest.

AI CEOs recognize the claims of humanity openly. In March 2023 and in multiple interviews since then, Altman laid out a “dream scenario” that “every person on Earth would come together, have a really thoughtful, deliberative conversation about where we want to draw the boundary on this system, and we would have something like the U.S. Constitutional Convention, where we debate the issues and we look at things from different perspectives.” To the question “Why pace?” Amodei answered that “society must have a say in how this technology is used” and that pacing would buy time for “public deliberations.” He did not say which society he had in mind. It cannot be America alone, or even the West in general — a technology with global consequences calls for a global deliberation.

Of course, humanity has no voice of its own in the existing international order. But we could give it one through careful design.

Our proposal is a standing global citizens’ assembly of 1,000 people chosen by lot from around the world — call it the Global Citizens’ Assembly on AI. This assembly would be charged with helping to set the purposes and limits of powerful AI, and with receiving the evaluators’ findings on whether those limits are kept. What must AI never be allowed to do? What do we want it to do for us and for those who come after us? Who should govern it, and by which principles? These are questions to be answered by humanity as a whole, and short of that a representative sample of it. Read Noema in print.

Humanity alone stands above AI CEOs, the governments in Washington and Beijing, other competing nations, international boards of experts and even the U.N. in its credibility to say ‘Stop!'”

The assembly would sit continuously rather than produce a single report. Members would serve fixed, part-time terms, with a third of the seats regularly redrawn by lot, so that the body keeps its memory without hardening into a class of its own. While they serve, members would deliberate over months, online and with local support, with financial compensation for their time and expenses, translation and interpretation, secure communication, and protection for those whose governments may dislike what they say. An independent civic secretariat would pool disclosed funding from participating governments and labs without letting funders influence recruitment or tamper with evidence.

Members could commission competing expertise, and anyone outside the assembly would have a published route to challenge its selection and its findings. Ideally, the assembly would also be connected to local and national processes whose input would feed into its deliberations. Earlier versions of these designs appeared in Fortune in 2023 and in Noema this August.

Why 1,000 global citizens? Is this not unwieldy? If basic demographic representativeness were the sole goal, a statistician might settle for a few hundred members. We ask for 1,000 for a different reason: symbolism and the salience that comes with size. A body the size of a large parliament is not a focus group, and cannot simply be ignored. A CEO can shrug off a critic, even a panel of experts. But any lab leader who refuses to answer a thousand people drawn by lot from every continent has to refuse on the planetary stage, in public, with reasons — and explain why the voice of humanity, in whose name they keep saying they are developing AI, does not, in fact, matter to them.

As to the unwieldiness, we believe careful facilitation and the judicious deployment of AI tools can make it a nonissue. The 1,000 people could be convened on a virtual platform and the deliberations broken down into small-group discussions followed by different styles of plenary meetings with expert testimonies. Organizers of virtual deliberative polls already know how to run these kinds of meetings efficiently and productively. Meanwhile, AI tools can translate, sort contributions and help members see both where they disagree and where they overlap. Members would keep the authority to judge the summaries, change the agenda and reject the machine’s account of what they meant.

Why choose the participants by lot from every continent rather than rely on a delegation of elected national representatives from every state? Because the stake of any person in the AI race is not conditional on knowledge, credentials or the ability to be elected. Nor is it conditional on the person’s nationality. People who are rarely asked about AI would sit as members of this assembly: the young, the rural, the illiterate, the unconnected, those whose governments would never send them.

To be sure, a lottery does not instantly turn a thousand people into a body legitimately representative of humanity. The assembly would have to earn its moral authority by being exemplary in its procedures and deliberations. Its moral authority would harden into political legitimacy as lawful institutions willingly recognize and take on duties toward it.

The duty to answer, in particular, is the key. Each recommendation from the assembly would go to a named institution, such as a lab or government, with a deadline to respond in public: what it accepts, what it rejects and why. Anyone could challenge a published refusal. Law or enforceable agreement would fix the obligation in advance, as an invitation to advise means nothing when the recipient can ignore it.

One jurisdiction already has enforcement powers of this kind. Since August, the EU’s AI Office can fine a frontier-model provider or order mitigations or a recall. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI have all signed the safety and security chapter of the code of practice that spells out what compliance looks like. Under it, each lab defines its own risk tiers, judges for itself whether its risks are acceptable and picks its own outside evaluators against criteria it publishes.

“Any lab leader who refuses to answer a thousand people drawn by lot from every continent has to refuse on the planetary stage, in public, with reasons — and explain why the voice of humanity, in whose name they keep saying they are developing AI, does not, in fact, matter to them.”

But in this system, each lab reports to the regulator in full, while the public gets summaries, and only “if and insofar as necessary.” Public consultation comes last among eight ways a lab may gather information, after web searches and market analyses. The most developed safety regime in law to date still treats the public as an input rather than a party. Our proposal would make the global public a party, and the EU could make that enforceable: A clause in a revised code of practice obliging signatories to answer a global assembly’s recommendations in public would give the duty to answer its first legal anchor, in a market no frontier lab can afford to leave.

But what about Beijing? The Chinese Communist Party has repeatedly denounced “exclusive groups” in AI governance, a thinly veiled reference to U.S.-led coalitions, and it has built its own multilateral frameworks, from its Global AI Governance Initiative to a World AI Cooperation Organization launched this summer in Shanghai. A body drawn by lot from every continent is the least Western-dominated forum on offer: By population alone, roughly one seat in six would belong to someone living in China. Beijing may still refuse to let these people take their seats. But the assembly does not need Beijing’s permission to change the game. Washington’s case against restraint rests on the claim that Beijing would never hold its post; a standing body to which people from both sides are invited, and before which each government is asked to answer publicly, turns that claim into a testable one. If Beijing stays away, the world will notice the distance between its rhetoric of inclusive governance and its conduct. If it participates, and, for example, opens its own labs to evaluators vetted under rules the assembly sets, the hunt for the stag has its two most important hunters in the same room.

Key parts of this proposal have been tried. More than 800 deliberative bodies similar to the one we propose have been convened around the world, according to the OECD. There exist several precedents at the global level. In 2021, the Global Assembly for COP26 drew 100 people by a worldwide location lottery to deliberate on climate change before the Glasgow summit. The Metaverse Community Forum on Bullying and Harassment, run by Meta, Stanford’s Deliberative Democracy Lab and the Behavioural Insights Team, convened more than 6,300 people across 32 countries and nine regions of the world in December 2022. In 2023, Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project asked about a thousand Americans to draft principles for an Anthropic model. In March 2024, Taiwan’s Ministry of Digital Affairs, which was led by one of the authors of this essay, worked with the Collective Intelligence Project to text 200,000 random numbers and bring 447 people online to deliberate on AI and information integrity.

How do we get from here to there? We can start with the willing.

First, a small coalition of governments and foundations can fund the assembly through an independent civic secretariat that convenes it on the terms above. That alone would create a focal point no lab or state controls.

Second, Anthropic has committed to letting embedded evaluators publish without its editorial control, and OpenAI has promised to follow. Both could go further: open their labs to evaluators vetted under rules the assembly sets, route what those evaluators find to the assembly, and accept a duty to answer it, on the record and within a fixed deadline, stating what they accept, what they reject and why. Labs that accept this would go a long way toward settling the inner race among themselves and change the outer one: Washington’s restraint would no longer be a unilateral gift to Beijing, but a verified, conditional offer, made before a witness, that Beijing is invited to join.

Third, participating labs can make pacing measurable now. They could pilot a transparent safety-research budget of 5% to 20% of their compute, under published accounting rules, alongside explicit limits on the compute used to accelerate capability research — giving evaluators something concrete to check. A separate allocation could fund public-use computing, with affected communities choosing the projects and judging what they are worth. No public benefit could be traded for a breach of a safety limit.

Is there enough time? If we start today, a first cohort can be seated by spring and deliberating through the rest of 2027. Urgency should not be an excuse to short-circuit public deliberation, and frontier development must stay answerable to it. And if it turns out the end of the world is not as imminent as predicted, and critics are right that the hype merely serves lucrative public offerings, we will still have built a way for humanity to take up, together, the problems that belong to all of it, from AI to climate, terrorism and migration.

Three CEOs have said the frontier must be paced. The racers cannot decide that pace alone; they need a witness they all trust. Let the people be that witness: Give them a seat, a say in the terms and a right to an answer. We should build the assembly now, while we can still set the terms.

stories.title: Orphaned by Diplomacy
stories.summary: Children are paying for wars they didn't start. The post Orphaned by Diplomacy appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

Every war produces its own vocabulary of loss—death tolls, displacement figures, damage assessments. But one number cuts across every current conflict and rarely makes the headline: the count of children who go to sleep each night with no parent left to tuck them in.

In Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine, and Iran, a generation of children is being orphaned at a pace the world has stopped finding shocking. What connects these children is not geography or ideology. It’s the absence of the diplomacy that might have kept their parents alive.

In Sudan and Gaza

Nowhere has the scale of child loss been more visible than in Gaza. UNICEF says that 58,000 children in Gaza have lost one or both parents, while more than a million children require protection and psychosocial support because of the war. The International Rescue Committee has separately estimated that between 15,000 and 19,000 children have been orphaned outright, with roughly 17,000 children unaccompanied or separated from their parents.

These aren’t abstractions. Extended families—grandparents, aunts, uncles, older siblings barely out of childhood themselves—are absorbing children who have nowhere else to go, in a territory where the infrastructure around housing, food, and medical care is itself in collapse. The scale is unprecedented enough that aid workers now describe it, without hyperbole, as the largest orphan crisis of modern times.

In Sudan, meanwhile, a civil war now past its three-year mark has become the world’s largest displacement crisis, and children are absorbing the brunt of it. More than 4 million children have been forced from their homes since the war began in April 2023, including nearly 1 million who crossed into neighboring countries. At least 42,000 unaccompanied and separated children have been registered inside Sudan and in neighboring countries, according to the UN’s refugee agency.

The casualty numbers keep climbing even as international attention fades. The UN has verified more than 5,700 grave violations against children across Sudan since the war’s onset, affecting over 5,100 children, more than 4,300 of whom have been killed or maimed—with drone strikes now accounting for nearly 80 percent of the killings and injuries this year . Behind each of those figures is a child who has lost the adults who were supposed to keep them safe, with nowhere near enough capacity to register, trace, or care for them all.

Ukraine and Iran

Russia’s war on Ukraine doesn’t produce the same daily casualty spikes as Gaza or Sudan, but four years in, its toll on children is cumulative and corrosive. More than a third of Ukraine’s children— nearly 2.6 million —remain displaced as the war enters its fifth year, including almost 1.8 million living as refugees outside the country. June 2026 recorded the highest number of child casualties in a single month since the invasion began, and more than 3,200 children have been killed or injured since February 2022. Add to that the children forcibly relocated into Russia, whose numbers UNICEF itself says it cannot fully verify, and Ukraine’s ledger of orphaned and separated children keeps growing in the dark.

Any honest accounting of children orphaned by war in 2026 has to include the U.S. and Israeli air campaign against Iran that opened in February. Over 40 days, the U.S. and Israel struck more than 17,000 targets inside Iran —a pace of warfare without modern precedent. Iranian officials say that 208 children were killed in the strikes, 168 of them in a single attack on a girls’ school in Minab. Thirteen of the children killed were under five, including a three-day-old newborn.

This is the piece of the puzzle that too often goes missing from the American conversation about these wars: Washington is not a bystander commenting on other people’s conflicts. It is frequently a co-belligerent, and Iranian children have paid for that war exactly as Sudanese, Gazan, and Ukrainian children paid for theirs.

When Diplomacy Fails

None of these wars was inevitable. Each had—has—an off-ramp that political leaders on multiple sides declined to take. Sudan’s rival generals could have been pressured into a ceasefire years ago. Gaza’s war could have ended with the earlier hostage-and-ceasefire frameworks that were left on the table. Ukraine’s war has had multiple negotiating windows quietly closed. Iran’s war was, by any reasonable definition, a war of choice. In every case, the children who will spend the next decade in foster care, extended-family homes, or institutional care had no vote in any of it.

When a parent dies, the paperwork of survival usually falls to whoever is left —an aunt, an older brother, a widow, a grandfather. Increasingly, these people are turning to crowdfunding platforms like GoFundMe and Chuffed because formal aid simply cannot reach them fast enough. One widowed mother of four in Gaza, ages ten months to eight years, has been raising money online after her husband died while trying to provide for the family—and after an earlier attempt to get help left her defrauded by someone posing as a helper. Another Gaza campaign is run by a man supporting 24 people on his own : his own five children, his late brothers’ 18 orphaned children, his wife, and his elderly mother, with no income left after losing his businesses to the war.

These campaigns rarely raise more than a few thousand dollars each. They are not a policy response. They are what happens when the policy response doesn’t come.

The Size of the Gap

Amid the caseload, Human Appeal has built one of the more durable responses to child orphanhood in conflict zones. The charity’s child welfare programs currently support more than 50,000 orphans across 14 countries, including tens of thousands of children in Gaza. Its annual comedy tours—now in their eleventh year and expanded across the UK, United States, and Canada—have become an unlikely but effective fundraising engine: in one landmark year, a single tour raised more than £1.75 million in pledges for the charity’s winter appeal, and the tradition still draws crowds in the thousands at individual stops.

The hope is real. So is the shortfall. Right now, Human Appeal says that more than 10,000 children across Gaza, Sudan, and thirteen other countries are registered and waiting for a sponsor . A night of laughter can fund school fees and food parcels for the children already in the program. It cannot, on its own, close a waitlist that keeps growing every time another ceasefire fails to hold.

Human Appeal, GoFundMe widows, Chuffed campaigns, and a hundred smaller efforts like them prove that ordinary people will show up for orphaned children when institutions won’t. What they can’t do is substitute for the diplomacy that would have kept those children’s parents alive in the first place. Comedy tours can chip away at a crisis. Only an end to the wars can stop it from growing.

stories.body:
The US relationship is stabilising, but how will Europe face up to Russia and China if President Le Pen is in power?

I addressed a group of more than 100 European ambassadors recently on the big challenges facing the continent this year and next. My main point to these senior diplomats was that, perhaps counterintuitively, Europe’s biggest external challenges over the next 12 months will come from Russia and China, rather than the US.

Europe’s relationship with Trump’s America remains difficult. The US president has weakened confidence in Nato, raised new transatlantic trade tensions and introduced uncertainty into everything from US support for Ukraine to his territorial designs on Greenland. Yet paradoxically, and notwithstanding Trump’s latest tariff threats over the EU’s outreach to Canada, the transatlantic relationship is becoming the more stable part of Europe’s external environment. Not stable, but more stable.

Compared with Russia and China, Europe’s disputes with Washington remain somewhat bounded – and largely negotiable. Ukraine’s rapidly expanding drone capabilities, its military innovation and battlefield experience have made Kyiv a more valuable partner for Washington. US defence companies are also benefiting from Europe’s military support for Ukraine and rearmament against Russia. The US, Denmark and Greenland now say they have struck a deal to allow the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland. The devil will be in the detail, but they have much stronger incentives to reach an accommodation than to allow the issue to become a lasting source of confrontation.

Trade tensions more broadly will persist, particularly over European regulation of American tech companies. The same is true of Nato, which has lost credibility because of Trump’s frequent admonishments. Nonetheless, these disputes are among countries with deeply interconnected security and economic interests. The risks posed to Europe by Russia and China are more structural – and increasingly point towards escalation.

Russia is becoming more dangerous because it is becoming weaker. The Kremlin is running out of cheap and politically painless ways to finance its war in Ukraine. Its original budget assumptions for 2026 have been overtaken by events. Military spending continues to rise, driven not only by the need for equipment but by the growing cost of recruiting soldiers for the frontline and paying compensation to casualties.

How Vladimir Putin funds his war is now the battlefield behind the battlefield. Further tax increases would damage an economy that, outside the military sector, is approaching recession. Borrowing has become more expensive, while public spending – on everything from schools and hospitals to infrastructure – is being squeezed to preserve the war effort.

Rather than push Putin towards compromise, Russia’s economic challenges are likely, initially at least, to produce the opposite effect. If he expects his economic position to worsen next year, the Kremlin has a powerful incentive to improve its military position now. That means escalation in Ukraine and against Nato. This explains the recent impromptu visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe.

In Ukraine, Russia is likely to accelerate its mobilisation efforts and engage in heavier attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, intensifying its efforts to undermine Ukraine’s economy and civilian morale this winter. The coming months will also see an escalation of Russia’s hybrid warfare activity against Nato countries.

China presents a different but equally serious challenge . For years, Europe has debated whether China is competing fairly. That argument is essentially over. A broad consensus now exists that China’s subsidies, industrial overcapacity, undervalued exchange rate and export-led economic model require a political response . The question is no longer whether Europe should defend itself against unfair Chinese competition, but how far it is prepared to go.

Beijing, meanwhile, has reached a very different conclusion. It increasingly sees Europe’s trade-defence measures, industrial policy and economic security agenda as an attempt to constrain China’s growth.

The European commissioner for trade and economic security, Maroš Šefčovič, and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, met in late June and committed to resolving a number of outstanding issues by October. That may delay confrontation. It is unlikely to avert it.

China is not going to abandon its use of industrial subsidies, the exchange rate or its export-led growth model. These are central features of China’s economic-strategy, and not subject to negotiation. Equally, the EU is not going to retreat from its economic security agenda. The union is developing investment controls, procurement restrictions and new industrial and trade-defence instruments. Although formally country-agnostic, many are clearly directed towards China.

Every European measure to reduce dependence on China is therefore likely to prompt a Chinese response, while every Chinese retaliation will strengthen the political case in Brussels to go further. That makes compromise harder, and escalation between the two sides more likely over the medium term.

after newsletter promotion

The most likely outcome is managed confrontation, rather than a full-scale trade war. The EU will expand targeted restrictions limiting China’s access in additional sectors. China will respond with selective tariffs, procurement barriers, regulatory pressure on European companies and tighter controls on critical minerals. Both sides will try to increase pressure without losing control.

Europe has leverage, too. China remains extraordinarily dependent on access to the EU single market, one of the world’s last large and wealthy export destinations. Europe can withstand coercion – if its governments remain united.

That is why France’s presidential election next year could prove more consequential for Europe than any decision taken in Washington, Moscow or Beijing. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen has a credible path to victory. She is scoring 35% to 38% in first-round polling at present, and is a more formidable candidate than her younger lieutenant, Jordan Bardella, who many assumed would be the Rassemblement National’s candidate in next year’s race. Her prospects will depend heavily on whether France’s fragmented centre can unite behind a single candidate. If it cannot, Le Pen could face the hard-left renegade Jean-Luc Mélenchon in the second round – and would probably win.

A Le Pen presidency would be profoundly disruptive for Europe. She would probably oppose further support for Ukraine, obstruct sanctions against Russia, undermine the bloc’s approach to China and initiate battles with Brussels over Schengen, fiscal rules, electricity pricing and the single market. Her threat to withhold France’s contribution to the EU budget could plunge the union into an unprecedented financial and constitutional crisis.

Europe’s external challenges, while substantial, are manageable. But the decisive variable is Europe itself: whether it can maintain the political coherence required to deal with the US, Russia and China. A Le Pen victory would call that coherence into question, precisely when Europe needs it most.

Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firm
